text:
<meta>This page continues the confession of the Venerable Sariputta, who is responding to a false accusation of offending a fellow monk. He uses a series of similes to demonstrate his humble and disciplined state of mind.</meta>

### The Numerical Discourses of the Buddha: The Elevens

Just as, venerable sir, a dusting-cloth <note>original: "rajoharaṇaṃ"</note> wipes up what is clean and wipes up what is unclean, wipes up excrement, wipes up urine, wipes up saliva, wipes up pus, and wipes up blood, yet the dusting-cloth is not troubled, ashamed, or disgusted by it: even so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a dusting-cloth, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Only one who has not established mindfulness of the body <note>original: "kāyagatā sati"</note> would, after offending a fellow monk here, set out on a journey without making amends.

Just as, venerable sir, a youth of the outcaste class <note>original: "caṇḍālakumārako"</note> or a maiden of the outcaste class, carrying a begging-basket and dressed in rags, enters a village or a town with a lowly heart: even so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like an outcaste youth, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Only one who has not established mindfulness of the body would, after offending a fellow monk here, set out on a journey without making amends.

Just as, venerable sir, a bull with its horns cut off, gentle, well-tamed, and well-trained, wanders from street to street and crossroad to crossroad without harming anyone with its feet or its horns: even so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like a bull with its horns cut off, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Only one who has not established mindfulness of the body would, after offending a fellow monk here, set out on a journey without making amends.

Just as, venerable sir, a woman or a man, young and fond of ornaments, having bathed their head, would be [horrified] <note>the sentence breaks here; the context implies being horrified by a carcass</note> by the carcass of a snake or...

8. Some manuscripts read "caṇḍāla boy" or "caṇḍāla girl."
13. Variant: "surato" meaning well-delighted or gentle.
</margin>

<summary>The Venerable Sariputta defends his conduct through similes of a dusting-cloth, an outcaste youth, and a de-horned bull. He emphasizes that his disciplined mind is incapable of knowingly offending others without seeking forgiveness.</summary>
